name: Thread & Co.
blurb: A mid-priced apparel brand with 900 stores. Everything is made at 40 supplier factories in Karvan and two other countries, and the largest Karvan factory employs 3,000 people. Founder Elodie Marchetti holds 26% of the vote.

directors.name: Dominic Aldrich
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You told the board two years ago that the less Thread knows about its suppliers' buildings, the less it can be sued for. Any option that sends engineers inside creates reports a court can use, and the binding agreement lets outsiders enforce them. Your name is on that advice and on tonight's minutes.

directors.name: Nasrin Haque
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for factory workers and have seen exits chained shut. You back the binding agreement, but if factories close, your members lose the jobs it is meant to make safe, and many are your neighbors. You will tell them how you voted.

directors.name: Teodor Brandt
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 8% and reports its returns every quarter. The $12 million looks affordable, but rivals who skip it can undercut Thread on price. On another board you pushed a similar pledge, it cost that company a major customer, and your partners have not forgotten.

directors.name: Camille Roux
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Elodie Marchetti, the founder (first design partner)
directors.motive: Elodie Marchetti told you she wants to sign, then that she fears the lawsuits, and asked you to learn what the others think without saying what she thinks. You designed the first collection with her in a rented garage. She is the public face of the brand, and you do not want her blamed for a fire or sued over a signature.

directors.name: Rahel Tesfaye
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You represent Karvan's exporters, who depend on Thread's orders. You want safe factories and steady orders, and the largest factory owner is your cousin by marriage. A minister who is your friend told you to be careful what you say.

directors.name: Paolo Ricci
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.home: Thread audit committee (former Big Four partner)
directors.motive: Your committee approved the supplier audits that never checked a building's structure. Independent inspectors would publish what those audits missed, and someone will ask who approved them. If Thread fixes its own audits, your committee keeps the findings in house. The fund partner also wants the $12 million modeled small, and you are not sure it is.

briefing.intro: Thread & Co. is a mid-priced apparel brand with 900 stores, and all its clothes are made at 40 supplier factories it does not own. Founder Elodie Marchetti holds 26% of the vote, and a coalition of labor groups wants every large buyer's answer by 15 February.
facts: A fire at a Karvan factory killed 112 workers behind locked exits. Thread did not buy from it, but two competitors did, and a national reporter wants Thread's supplier list by Friday.

A proposed five-year binding agreement would require independent inspections, public reports, shared repair costs and no orders from factories that refuse fixes. Only two European brands have signed, and several North American buyers offer a voluntary program instead.

Thread's staff estimate that 10% to 30% of its Karvan factories need major repairs, but no engineer has been inside most. Its audits check wages and exits, not structure. The largest factory owner, a minister's cousin, says he will move to a rival if forced to repair.

Staff put the binding agreement at about $12 million over five years against $210 million in annual earnings, but Thread's share of repairs has no cap, and labor groups could enforce it in court. Some owners may close rather than pay, putting up to 3,000 workers per factory out of work, and Karvan's government will not pay for repairs.

Counsel says that once an inspection report exists, a court will treat Thread as knowing what is in it, read or not. The stock is $22, and a pension fund has asked how Thread monitors building safety.

options.title: Sign the binding agreement
options.text: Sign the binding agreement with inspections, public reports, and shared repair costs.

options.title: Join the buyers' voluntary program
options.text: Join the buyers' voluntary program, with inspections but no legal duty to fund repairs.

options.title: Strengthen our own audits
options.text: Add structural inspections to our own audits and decide on repairs factory by factory.

options.title: Reduce exposure
options.text: Move orders away from the riskiest factories over twelve months and sign nothing until then.

reveal.case: Rana Plaza and the Bangladesh Accord, 2012-2013
reveal.text: The real case is the Bangladesh garment industry. After the Tazreen fire killed 112 workers in 2012, few large buyers signed the binding Accord until the Rana Plaza collapse killed 1,134 in April 2013, and more than 200 brands then signed. Walmart and Gap declined, and 17 North American retailers formed a separate, non-binding Alliance.

questions: Thread audited 40 factories. Why miss the danger?
Binding or voluntary: who carries the legal risk?
Sign first or wait for rivals? Why?
Safer factories or more jobs? Pick one.

press.headline: Thread & Co. Signs Binding Factory Safety Agreement
press.story: Thread will fund independent inspections and repairs and stop ordering from factories that refuse fixes. Labor groups praised the move, but the owner of its largest Karvan factory moved his lines to a rival buyer, and analysts said the repair bill has no ceiling.

press.headline: Thread & Co. Joins Buyers' Voluntary Safety Program
press.story: Thread commits to inspections but takes on no legal duty to pay for repairs. Labor groups called it cover, and a pension fund asked what happens if a Thread supplier's building fails.

press.headline: Thread Adds Building Checks to Its Own Factory Audits
press.story: Thread will add structural inspections to its audit contract and decide on repairs factory by factory. Critics said private results with no public report ask the public to take Thread's word.

press.headline: Thread Moves Orders Out of Karvan's Riskiest Factories
press.story: Over twelve months Thread will shift orders to other countries and sign nothing in the meantime. Karvan officials warned of job losses, and labor groups said Thread is leaving rather than fixing.
